## At a glance

**Guiding question:** How does a segmentation decision change the biological conclusion?\
**For:** researchers in pathology and translational immunology, doctoral researchers who analyse multiplex tissue
images, and reviewers of spatial analyses. · **Prerequisites:** the unit of analysis from @sec-b03; the measurement
chain and pseudoreplication from @sec-b10.\
**In the course:** [W4 · What imaging, gait and tissue models
measure](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w4-imaging-gait-tissue.html) (tissue
station) and [W5 · Causal questions, trajectories and
phenotypes](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w5-causality-trajectories-phenotypes.html)
· **Data:** synthetic (generated in the chapter) · **Core reading time:** about 10 minutes
:::

## Case and decision {#sec-b12-case}

A research pathologist in a fictitious translational group analyses multiplex immunofluorescence images of soft tissue
taken from the fracture site during surgery. Twelve patients are included: six whose fractures healed on schedule and
six with delayed healing. The hypothesis for a grant application is that T cells and macrophages are more often in
direct contact in delayed healing. The image-analysis pipeline finds nuclei with a pretrained segmentation model and
then grows every nucleus outwards by a fixed distance to approximate the cell boundary. The lab's default is 4 µm; a
colleague's older pipeline used 1 µm. With 4 µm, the share of T cells touching a macrophage is clearly higher in
delayed healing, and a test over all T cells gives p < 0.01. With 1 µm, the difference almost disappears. The
pathologist has to decide which result goes into the application, and what its sample size is. The first error in
this chapter is the segment boundary.

## Core reading {#sec-b12-core}

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Core reading** · recommended reading for W4 (tissue station) · about 10 minutes · ends before ‘Lab’
:::

**A chain of decisions.** A spatial tissue analysis is a long measurement chain (@fig-b12-chain). Tissue is cut into
sections a few micrometres thick and stained with several antibodies at once, for example a nuclear stain, CD3 for T
cells and CD68 for macrophages. A scanner records each channel as an image whose pixel size is given in micrometres.
A learning model, typically a pretrained network, then segments nuclei [@stringer2021cellpose;
@greenwald2022mesmer]. Because membranes are harder to see than nuclei, many pipelines approximate each cell by growing
its nucleus outwards by a fixed distance. Marker intensities are averaged within this boundary, a threshold assigns a
phenotype, and every cell becomes a point with a type. Only then does the neighbourhood analysis begin
[@schapiro2017histocat]. Every step contains a parameter, and the boundary expansion is one of the least visible.

```{r}
#| label: fig-b12-chain
#| fig-cap: "Measurement chain for a cell-contact analysis in multiplex tissue images. The dashed box marks the learning model (nucleus segmentation); grey boxes mark the reference and the decision. Units change from micrometres to cell types to shares. Independent unit for the group question: patient (n = 12, six per group). Synthetic case."
#| fig-alt: "Vertical flow chart with nine boxes: tissue from the fracture site; section and multiplex staining; scanner images; nucleus segmentation (dashed box, learning model); cell boundary by expansion; phenotype by marker threshold; contact measure; summary per patient; group comparison and decision. Notes on the right list the unit or reference for each step: section thickness in micrometres, staining run as batch, pixel size in micrometres, manual annotation as reference for segmentation, expansion distance in micrometres, single-stain controls, contact share in per cent with a permutation reference, the patient as the independent unit with n = 12."
#| fig-height: 6.6
#| code-fold: true
library(ggplot2)
# Generic drawing of a measurement chain: one box per step, a note per step, dashed border for the learning model
draw_chain <- function(steps, note_title = "Unit or reference") {
  steps$y <- rev(seq_len(nrow(steps)))
  types <- c("measurement", "reference", "model", "decision")
  ggplot(steps) +
    geom_segment(data = steps[-nrow(steps), ], aes(x = 1, xend = 1, y = y - 0.24, yend = y - 0.76),
                 arrow = grid::arrow(length = grid::unit(0.15, "cm")), colour = "grey30") +
    geom_tile(aes(x = 1, y = y, fill = type, linetype = type), width = 1.7, height = 0.5,
              colour = "grey20", linewidth = 0.5) +
    geom_text(aes(x = 1, y = y, label = label), size = 3.4) +
    geom_text(aes(x = 2.0, y = y, label = note), hjust = 0, size = 3.1, colour = "grey15") +
    annotate("text", x = 2.0, y = nrow(steps) + 0.55, label = note_title, hjust = 0, fontface = "bold",
             size = 3.2) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(measurement = "white", reference = "grey85", model = "#D9ECF7",
                                 decision = "grey70"), breaks = types, name = NULL) +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = c(measurement = "solid", reference = "solid", model = "dashed",
                                     decision = "solid"), breaks = types, name = NULL) +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0.1, 4.6)) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0.5, nrow(steps) + 0.8)) +
    theme_void(base_size = 11) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, colour = "#4D4D4D"))
}
chain_b12 <- data.frame(
  label = c("Tissue from fracture site", "Section and staining", "Scanner images", "Nucleus segmentation",
            "Cell boundary (expansion)", "Phenotype by threshold", "Contact measure", "Summary per patient",
            "Group comparison, decision"),
  note = c("12 patients, 3 fields each", "section thickness in µm; staining run = batch",
           "pixel size in µm per pixel; one channel per marker", "reference: manual annotation of a subset",
           "expansion e in µm (1 to 5 in the lab)", "reference: single-stain controls",
           "share of T cells in contact (%); permutation reference", "independent unit: patient, n = 12",
           "6 vs 6 patients"),
  type = c("measurement", "measurement", "measurement", "model", "measurement", "reference", "measurement",
           "measurement", "decision")
)
draw_chain(chain_b12) +
  labs(caption = "Synthetic case · independent unit: patient (n = 12)")
```

**Why the boundary matters.** Two cells count as being in contact when their segmented boundaries touch. With nuclei
of radius 3 µm and an expansion of $e$ µm on each side, that happens when the centres are at most $2(3 + e)$ µm apart:
8 µm for $e = 1$, 14 µm for $e = 4$. The area within reach of a cell grows with the square of that distance, so the
expansion has a large effect on the number of contacts (@fig-b12-field). It has a larger effect where cells are packed
more densely. In the synthetic data, tissue from delayed healing contains more cells per square millimetre. A wider
boundary therefore produces more chance contacts there, even though the T cells and macrophages are placed without any
attraction to each other. **The key assumption is that a contact between segmented boundaries reflects a contact
between real cells, to the same degree in both groups.** Denser tissue, thicker sections or a different staining run
can each break this assumption for one group only.

```{r}
#| label: b12-cells
#| echo: false
# Synthetic tissue: positions and cell types (the lab shows and checks this code step by step)
field_size <- 500        # field of view, µm per side
nucleus_radius <- 3      # µm
min_gap <- 7             # minimum distance between nucleus centres, µm
place_cells <- function(n, size = field_size, min_dist = min_gap) {
  x <- numeric(0); y <- numeric(0); tries <- 0
  while (length(x) < n && tries < 50 * n) {
    tries <- tries + 1
    cx <- runif(1, 0, size); cy <- runif(1, 0, size)
    if (length(x) == 0 || min((x - cx)^2 + (y - cy)^2) >= min_dist^2) { x <- c(x, cx); y <- c(y, cy) }
  }
  data.frame(x = x, y = y)
}
patients <- data.frame(patient = sprintf("T%02d", 1:12), group = rep(c("uneventful", "delayed"), each = 6))
patients$density <- ifelse(patients$group == "delayed", rnorm(12, 3000, 300), rnorm(12, 2200, 250))
cell_list <- list()
for (i in 1:12) for (f in 1:3) {
  n <- rpois(1, patients$density[i] * (field_size / 1000)^2)
  p <- place_cells(n)
  p$type <- sample(c("T cell", "macrophage", "other"), nrow(p), replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.15, 0.15, 0.70))
  p$patient <- patients$patient[i]; p$group <- patients$group[i]; p$field <- f
  cell_list[[length(cell_list) + 1]] <- p
}
cells <- do.call(rbind, cell_list)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-b12-field
#| fig-cap: "A 120 µm × 120 µm detail of one synthetic field of view from a patient with delayed healing, chosen as the detail with the most contacts at 4 µm. Filled discs: nuclei (radius 3 µm; triangles mark T cells, squares macrophages); grey outlines: cell boundaries after expansion by 1 µm (left) or 4 µm (right); thick lines: T cell–macrophage pairs counted as in contact. Unit: µm. Synthetic data; the independent unit for the study is the patient (n = 12)."
#| fig-alt: "Two square panels showing the same tissue detail of 120 by 120 micrometres with about forty cells. Triangles mark T cells, squares macrophages and small grey discs other cells; each cell is surrounded by a circular outline. In the left panel, expansion 1 micrometre, outlines are small and almost no T cell touches a macrophage. In the right panel, expansion 4 micrometres, outlines are larger, many touch or overlap, and several thick lines connect T cells with neighbouring macrophages."
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| code-fold: true
# Choose the 120 µm x 120 µm detail of patient T07, field 1, that contains the most contacts at 4 µm
field_t07 <- cells[cells$patient == "T07" & cells$field == 1, ]
count_links <- function(w, e) {
  t_idx <- which(w$type == "T cell"); m_idx <- which(w$type == "macrophage")
  if (length(t_idx) == 0 || length(m_idx) == 0) return(0)
  g <- expand.grid(t = t_idx, m = m_idx)
  sum(sqrt((w$x[g$t] - w$x[g$m])^2 + (w$y[g$t] - w$y[g$m])^2) <= 2 * (nucleus_radius + e))
}
origins <- expand.grid(x0 = seq(0, field_size - 120, by = 20), y0 = seq(0, field_size - 120, by = 20))
origins$links <- apply(origins, 1, function(o) count_links(
  field_t07[field_t07$x >= o[1] & field_t07$x < o[1] + 120 & field_t07$y >= o[2] & field_t07$y < o[2] + 120, ], 4))
best <- origins[which.max(origins$links), ]
window <- field_t07[field_t07$x >= best$x0 & field_t07$x < best$x0 + 120 &
                      field_t07$y >= best$y0 & field_t07$y < best$y0 + 120, ]
window$x <- window$x - best$x0   # local coordinates of the detail
window$y <- window$y - best$y0
circle <- function(x, y, r, id) {
  a <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 41)
  data.frame(id = id, x = x + r * cos(a), y = y + r * sin(a))
}
panels <- lapply(c(1, 4), function(e) {
  label <- paste0("expansion ", e, " µm")
  outlines <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(window)), function(k)
    circle(window$x[k], window$y[k], nucleus_radius + e, k)))
  nuclei <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(window)), function(k)
    cbind(circle(window$x[k], window$y[k], nucleus_radius, k), type = window$type[k])))
  t_idx <- which(window$type == "T cell"); m_idx <- which(window$type == "macrophage")
  pairs <- expand.grid(t = t_idx, m = m_idx)
  pairs <- pairs[sqrt((window$x[pairs$t] - window$x[pairs$m])^2 + (window$y[pairs$t] - window$y[pairs$m])^2) <=
                   2 * (nucleus_radius + e), ]
  links <- data.frame(x = window$x[pairs$t], y = window$y[pairs$t], xend = window$x[pairs$m],
                      yend = window$y[pairs$m])
  list(outlines = cbind(outlines, panel = label), nuclei = cbind(nuclei, panel = label),
       links = if (nrow(links) > 0) cbind(links, panel = label) else NULL,
       centres = cbind(window, panel = label))
})
pick <- function(part) do.call(rbind, lapply(panels, `[[`, part))
type_levels <- c("T cell", "macrophage", "other")
centres <- pick("centres"); centres$type <- factor(centres$type, levels = type_levels)
nuclei <- pick("nuclei"); nuclei$type <- factor(nuclei$type, levels = type_levels)
ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = pick("outlines"), aes(x, y, group = id), fill = NA, colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_polygon(data = nuclei, aes(x, y, group = id, fill = type), colour = NA) +
  geom_segment(data = pick("links"), aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend), linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(data = centres[centres$type != "other", ], aes(x, y, shape = type), size = 1.6, colour = "black") +
  facet_wrap(~ panel) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("T cell" = unname(cdsr_colours["orange"]),
                               macrophage = unname(cdsr_colours["blue"]), other = "grey80"), name = NULL) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("T cell" = 17, macrophage = 15), name = NULL) +
  guides(shape = "none") +                       # triangles = T cells, squares = macrophages (see caption)
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 120), ylim = c(0, 120), expand = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "x (µm)", y = "y (µm)",
       caption = "Synthetic tissue · patient T07, field 1 · triangles: T cells, squares: macrophages") +
  theme_cdsr() +
  theme(panel.spacing = grid::unit(1.5, "lines"))
```

**Units and the learning step.** The units change several times along the chain. Section thickness and distances are
micrometres; positions in the image are pixels and become micrometres only through the scanner's pixel size; cell
density is given in cells per square millimetre; the contact measure is a share of T cells. Confusing pixels with
micrometres is a silent error, because every number still looks plausible. The learning model sits at the
segmentation step. It was trained on other images, often of other tissues and stains. In dense infiltrates, touching
nuclei can be merged into one cell or split into two, and that changes cell counts and contacts precisely in the
group with the higher density. The segmentation model therefore needs the same scrutiny as the expansion parameter
that follows it: its name, version and weights belong in the methods, and its errors should be checked in both groups
separately.

**What counts as a reference.** Each step needs its own check. Segmentation is checked against a pathologist's manual
annotation of a subset of fields, made without knowing the patient's group. Phenotype thresholds are checked with
single-stain controls. For the contact measure itself, the natural reference is what density alone would produce: if
the cell types are shuffled at random among the same positions, how often would a T cell touch a macrophage? Comparing
the observed share with this permutation expectation separates a specific neighbourhood preference from simple crowding
[@schapiro2017histocat].

**Two pipelines, two conclusions.** The colleague's 1 µm and the lab's 4 µm are both defensible defaults. Neither is
right in itself; which one approximates real cell boundaries is an empirical question for the manual reference above.
What is not defensible is choosing between them after seeing which gives the larger group difference. The expansion
belongs in the analysis plan, fixed after a blinded check against manual boundaries, and the results for a range of
expansions belong in the supplement as a sensitivity analysis.

**Count patients, not cells.** The study images tens of thousands of cells, but the independent unit is the patient.
Cells from the same patient share genetics, treatment, surgery and staining; they are pseudoreplicates
[@zimmerman2021pseudoreplication]. Tests that treat every cell as independent produce false discoveries even in the
absence of a biological difference [@squair2021pseudobulk]. Two further pitfalls sit at the edges of the chain. Cells
near the border of a field of view have neighbours outside the image that are not counted, which lowers their apparent
number of contacts; spatial statistics handle this with edge corrections [@baddeley2005spatstat]. And if the two
groups were stained in different runs, a batch effect in staining intensity can shift phenotypes in one group only
[@leek2010batch], the same structure as the lamp in @sec-b10.

**Question for the workshop:** Which number would you report as the sample size for the contact comparison, and which
single additional analysis would show whether more contacts in delayed healing mean more than more cells?

## Lab {#sec-b12-lab}

The lab generates twelve fictitious patients with three fields of view each, varies the boundary expansion, recomputes
the contact share, compares it with a permutation reference and condenses everything per patient. In the synthetic
truth there is no attraction between T cells and macrophages; only the cell density differs between the groups.

**Step 1 – the synthetic tissue.** The cells were already placed in a hidden chunk of the core reading, because the
figure there needs them. Its code is repeated here without being run again: nucleus centres at least 7 µm apart (a
simple hard-core process), 15% T cells, 15% macrophages and 70% other cells, assigned at random, and a higher cell
density in delayed healing.

```{r}
#| label: b12-cells-shown
#| ref.label: b12-cells
#| eval: false
```

Then we check the design.

```{r}
#| label: b12-design
cells_per_field <- aggregate(x ~ patient + group + field, data = cells, FUN = length)
names(cells_per_field)[4] <- "cells"
density_per_patient <- aggregate(cells ~ patient + group, data = cells_per_field, FUN = mean)
density_per_patient$cells_per_mm2 <- density_per_patient$cells / (field_size / 1000)^2
aggregate(cells_per_mm2 ~ group, data = density_per_patient, FUN = mean)
min_distance <- tapply(seq_len(nrow(cells)), paste(cells$patient, cells$field), function(k)
  min(dist(cells[k, c("x", "y")])))
c(patients = length(unique(cells$patient)), fields = nrow(cells_per_field), cells = nrow(cells),
  t_cells = sum(cells$type == "T cell"))
stopifnot(length(unique(cells$patient)) == 12, nrow(cells_per_field) == 36, min(min_distance) >= min_gap)
```

**Step 2 – contacts for a given boundary.** For each field we list all pairs of cells whose centres are close enough
to touch at the largest expansion. The contact share for any expansion is then a filter on this list.

```{r}
#| label: b12-contacts
expansions <- 1:5                                        # boundary expansion in µm
max_reach <- 2 * (nucleus_radius + max(expansions))      # centre distance for contact at 5 µm
close_pairs <- function(d) {
  D <- as.matrix(dist(d[, c("x", "y")]))
  idx <- which(D <= max_reach & upper.tri(D), arr.ind = TRUE)
  data.frame(i = idx[, 1], j = idx[, 2], distance = D[idx])
}
# Share of T cells with at least one macrophage contact; 'edge' drops T cells whose reach crosses the border
contact_count <- function(d, pairs, e, types = d$type, edge = FALSE) {
  reach <- 2 * (nucleus_radius + e)
  p <- pairs[pairs$distance <= reach, ]
  t_cells <- which(types == "T cell")
  if (edge) t_cells <- t_cells[d$x[t_cells] > reach & d$x[t_cells] < field_size - reach &
                                 d$y[t_cells] > reach & d$y[t_cells] < field_size - reach]
  touching <- c(p$i[types[p$j] == "macrophage"], p$j[types[p$i] == "macrophage"])
  c(t_cells = length(t_cells), in_contact = sum(t_cells %in% touching))
}
```

**Step 3 – shift the boundary and build the permutation reference.** For every field and expansion we record the
observed contacts, the contacts after excluding T cells near the border, and the share expected if the cell types were
shuffled at random among the same positions (100 permutations per field).

```{r}
#| label: b12-shift
set.seed(2212)
field_keys <- unique(cells[, c("patient", "group", "field")])
per_field <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(field_keys)), function(k) {
  d <- cells[cells$patient == field_keys$patient[k] & cells$field == field_keys$field[k], ]
  pairs <- close_pairs(d)
  do.call(rbind, lapply(expansions, function(e) {
    observed <- contact_count(d, pairs, e)
    inner <- contact_count(d, pairs, e, edge = TRUE)
    shuffled <- replicate(100, { s <- contact_count(d, pairs, e, types = sample(d$type)); s[2] / s[1] })
    data.frame(field_keys[k, ], expansion = e, t_cells = observed[1], in_contact = observed[2],
               t_cells_inner = inner[1], in_contact_inner = inner[2], expected_share = mean(shuffled))
  }))
}))
# Condense per patient: pooled counts over the three fields
per_patient <- aggregate(cbind(t_cells, in_contact, t_cells_inner, in_contact_inner) ~ patient + group + expansion,
                         data = per_field, FUN = sum)
per_patient <- merge(per_patient, aggregate(expected_share ~ patient + expansion, data = per_field, FUN = mean))
per_patient$share <- per_patient$in_contact / per_patient$t_cells
per_patient$share_inner <- per_patient$in_contact_inner / per_patient$t_cells_inner
per_patient$ratio <- per_patient$share / per_patient$expected_share
# Contacts can only increase with a wider boundary, for every patient
monotone <- tapply(seq_len(nrow(per_patient)), per_patient$patient, function(k)
  all(diff(per_patient$share[k][order(per_patient$expansion[k])]) >= 0))
stopifnot(all(monotone))
round(aggregate(cbind(share, expected_share, ratio) ~ group + expansion, data = per_patient, FUN = mean)[, -1], 3)
```

**Step 4 – the same question at two levels.** For the colleague's 1 µm and the default 4 µm we test the group
difference once over all T cells, as if they were independent, and once with one value per patient.

```{r}
#| label: b12-tests
compare_levels <- function(e) {
  d <- per_patient[per_patient$expansion == e, ]
  pooled <- aggregate(cbind(in_contact, t_cells) ~ group, data = d, FUN = sum)
  data.frame(expansion_um = e,
             share_delayed = mean(d$share[d$group == "delayed"]),
             share_uneventful = mean(d$share[d$group == "uneventful"]),
             n_t_cells = sum(d$t_cells),
             p_cells = prop.test(pooled$in_contact, pooled$t_cells)$p.value,   # every T cell as a unit
             n_patients = nrow(d),
             p_patients = t.test(share ~ group, data = d)$p.value,            # one value per patient
             p_ratio = t.test(ratio ~ group, data = d)$p.value)                # density-adjusted
}
levels_test <- rbind(compare_levels(1), compare_levels(4))
levels_test
gap <- levels_test$share_delayed - levels_test$share_uneventful
stopifnot(gap[2] > gap[1], levels_test$n_t_cells[2] > 3000,
          levels_test$p_cells[2] < 0.01, levels_test$p_patients[2] > 0.05, levels_test$p_ratio[2] > 0.05)
```

At 1 µm the groups differ by `r cdsr_number(100 * gap[1], 1)` percentage points; at 4 µm by
`r cdsr_number(100 * gap[2], 1)` points. Only the boundary changed. The test over
`r cdsr_number(levels_test$n_t_cells[2])` T cells reports p = `r signif(levels_test$p_cells[2], 2)` at 4 µm; the test
over `r levels_test$n_patients[2]` patients reports p = `r signif(levels_test$p_patients[2], 2)`. The density-adjusted
ratio, observed divided by expected share, is close to 1 in both groups (p = `r signif(levels_test$p_ratio[2], 2)`):
the extra contacts in delayed healing are what crowding alone produces. @fig-b12-shift shows the whole range of
expansions.

```{r}
#| label: fig-b12-shift
#| fig-cap: "Left: share of T cells in contact with at least one macrophage, per patient (thin lines) and group mean (thick lines), against the boundary expansion in µm. Right: the same share divided by the share expected from random placement of cell types (permutation reference); 1 means no preference beyond density. Synthetic data; independent unit: patient (n = 12, six per group); 3 fields of 500 µm × 500 µm per patient."
#| fig-alt: "Two line charts with boundary expansion from 1 to 5 micrometres on the horizontal axis. Left panel: contact share from about 1 to 34 per cent rises steeply with expansion for every patient; the dashed group line for delayed healing rises faster than the solid line for uneventful healing, so the gap widens from under one to about five percentage points. Right panel: the ratio of observed to expected share stays close to 1 for both groups at every expansion, with individual patients scattering between about 0.6 and 1.8 at 1 micrometre and much less at larger expansions."
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| code-fold: true
long <- rbind(
  data.frame(per_patient[, c("patient", "group", "expansion")], value = 100 * per_patient$share,
             panel = "Contact share (% of T cells)"),
  data.frame(per_patient[, c("patient", "group", "expansion")], value = per_patient$ratio,
             panel = "Observed / expected share")
)
means <- aggregate(value ~ group + expansion + panel, data = long, FUN = mean)
ggplot(long, aes(expansion, value, colour = group, linetype = group)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = patient), linewidth = 0.3, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(data = means, linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_point(data = means, aes(shape = group), size = 2.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(cdsr_colours[c("red", "blue")])) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = cdsr_linetypes[c(2, 1)]) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = cdsr_shapes[c(2, 1)]) +
  labs(x = "Boundary expansion (µm)", y = NULL, colour = "Healing", linetype = "Healing", shape = "Healing",
       caption = "Synthetic data · n = 12 patients (6 per group) · 3 fields of 0.25 mm² each") +
  theme_cdsr()
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Reporting "n = `r cdsr_number(levels_test$n_t_cells[2])` T cells" as the sample size. Cells, fields and pixels are
measurements within patients. The sample size for a comparison between groups of patients is the number of patients;
the number of cells per patient describes the precision of each patient's value and belongs next to it.
:::

**Step 5 – what condensing per patient loses.** Condensing to one share per patient is what makes the test honest, but
it discards information that belongs in the report.

```{r}
#| label: b12-aggregation
at4 <- per_field[per_field$expansion == 4, ]
at4$share <- at4$in_contact / at4$t_cells
loss <- aggregate(cbind(t_cells, share) ~ patient + group, data = at4,
                  FUN = function(v) c(min = min(v), max = max(v)))
loss <- data.frame(patient = loss$patient, group = loss$group,
                   t_cells_total = per_patient$t_cells[per_patient$expansion == 4][match(loss$patient,
                                     per_patient$patient[per_patient$expansion == 4])],
                   field_share_min = round(loss$share[, "min"], 3), field_share_max = round(loss$share[, "max"], 3))
head(loss[order(-loss$t_cells_total), ], 4)
range(loss$t_cells_total)
```

Three things disappear in the patient summary. First, precision: the shares rest on between
`r min(loss$t_cells_total)` and `r max(loss$t_cells_total)` T cells per patient, so they are not equally reliable.
Second, heterogeneity: the three fields of one patient can differ by several percentage points, and a single field
with a dense aggregate can dominate. Third, the spatial arrangement itself: where in the tissue the contacts occur, for
example near vessels or at the fracture gap, is no longer visible. Reporting the number of T cells and fields per
patient, and the range across fields, keeps the loss transparent. Models that keep the cells but treat the patient as
the unit, such as generalised linear mixed models, are the next step ([Methods in R: glmer: Generalised Mixed
Models](https://cttir.github.io/methods-in-r/sec-ch-07-regression.html#sec-chapters-07-regression-glmer-generalized-mixed)).

::: {.callout-note title="Other implementation: Python with scikit-image and Cellpose"}
In practice the segmentation runs in Python. [scikit-image](https://scikit-image.org/docs/stable/) (0.26.0 in
November 2026) provides `skimage.segmentation.expand_labels(label_image, distance)`, which "expands labels in label
image by distance pixels without overlapping", and `skimage.measure.regionprops_table` for centroids and mean marker
intensities [@vanderwalt2014skimage]. The distance is given in pixels: at 0.5 µm per pixel, the lab's 4 µm become 8
pixels, and a pipeline that forgets the conversion silently doubles or halves the boundary. Nuclei are often found with
[Cellpose](https://cellpose.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) (4.2.1 in November 2026), a PyTorch-based generalist model
[@stringer2021cellpose; @paszke2019pytorch]; its current model uses the first three image channels and was trained on
objects of about 7.5 to 120 pixels in diameter, so channel order and pixel size must be documented. The concrete
advantage is a tested segmentation of real images, which this lab replaces by synthetic points. For a fair comparison
the following must be identical: pixel size, the label image, the expansion in µm, the contact definition (labels that
touch after expansion), the field borders and edge rule, and the per-patient aggregation. Because `expand_labels`
stops where two growing cells meet, a third cell between two others can block a contact that the distance rule in this
lab would count; the shares should therefore agree closely but not exactly, and the tolerance (for example one
percentage point per patient) has to be set beforehand. Status: conceptual comparison, not run.
:::

## Counter-check {#sec-b12-countercheck}

Predict first: if T cells whose reach crosses the border of the field are excluded, does the contact share rise or
fall, and does the conclusion of the group comparison change?

```{r}
#| label: b12-countercheck
edge_check <- aggregate(cbind(share, share_inner) ~ group, data = per_patient[per_patient$expansion == 4, ],
                        FUN = mean)
edge_check$t_cells_kept <- aggregate(t_cells_inner ~ group, data = per_patient[per_patient$expansion == 4, ],
                                     FUN = sum)$t_cells_inner
edge_check
d4 <- per_patient[per_patient$expansion == 4, ]
p_inner <- t.test(share_inner ~ group, data = d4)$p.value
stopifnot(all(edge_check$share_inner > edge_check$share), p_inner > 0.05)
```

The border correction raises the share slightly in both groups, because cells at the border lose neighbours that lie
outside the image. With 500 µm fields and a reach of 14 µm the effect is small and does not change the patient-level
result (p = `r signif(p_inner, 2)`). It grows with smaller fields and larger reach. A second counter-check is a thought
experiment that the lab has already answered: if both groups had the same cell density, the gap in contact share would
shrink towards zero at every expansion, which is what the observed/expected ratio in @fig-b12-shift shows.

The checkable measurement assumption of this case is: *the boundary expansion, converted to pixels with the scanner's
pixel size, reproduces a pathologist's manual cell boundaries in a blinded subset of fields of both groups equally
well*. The plausible failure mode is: *a default expansion chosen for sparse tissue creates chance contacts in dense
tissue and turns a difference in cellularity into an apparent difference in cell interaction*.

## Consequences for patients and operations {#sec-b12-consequences}

**A misleading sample size.** The most direct harm in this case is a number. "p < 0.01 in more than 3,000 T cells"
reads like strong evidence and can secure funding, steer a follow-up study and recruit further patients for tissue
donation, all for a difference that crowding explains. The honest statement is "12 patients, six per group, no
difference in density-adjusted contacts". Patients who donate tissue do so on the assumption that their samples are
analysed in a way that can answer the question.

**Wrong tissue interpretation.** If a contact score were later used to classify patients, for example as at risk of
delayed healing, the segmentation parameter would decide which patients receive closer follow-up or additional
procedures. Software that analyses images of tissue specimens to provide information on a pathological state may fall
under the In Vitro Diagnostic Medical Devices Regulation (EU) 2017/746, whose definition covers software intended to be
used in vitro for the examination of specimens derived from the human body [@eu2017ivdr; binding text]. Whether a
given tool is such a device depends on its intended purpose; the guidance MDCG 2019-11 Rev. 1 helps with the
qualification but is not binding [@mdcg2019-11]. @sec-b22 works through an IVD vignette.

**Data protection.** Whole-slide images linked with clinical data are health data. Rare combinations of diagnosis,
age and date of surgery can identify a patient even without a name; @sec-b23 and @sec-b26 discuss minimisation and
controlled access.

**Operations and integrity.** The expansion distance, the segmentation model and its version, the pixel size and the
phenotype thresholds are part of the result. They belong in the model passport (@sec-b27) and should be stored with a
checksum, so that a later re-analysis can show that it used the same parameters (@sec-b24).

## Look up and transfer {#sec-b12-lookup}

- **Reviewer question:** The manuscript reports a significant increase in T cell–macrophage contacts "in 4,812 cells".
  How many patients contributed, how was the cell boundary defined and in which unit, and was the contact frequency
  compared with what cell density alone would produce?
- **Self-test:** A second study uses the same pipeline but images only one field of 250 µm × 250 µm per patient, and the
  boundary expansion is set to 5 µm. Without computing: will the border effect be larger or smaller than in the lab,
  will the gap between dense and sparse tissue be larger or smaller, and what is the independent sample size if 20
  patients contribute 9,000 T cells?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The border effect will be larger. A smaller field has more cells near its border relative to its area, and the reach
grows to $2(3 + 5) = 16$ µm, so a larger share of T cells has neighbours outside the image. The gap between dense and
sparse tissue will also be larger, because a wider boundary produces more chance contacts where cells are packed more
tightly. The independent sample size is 20 patients; the 9,000 T cells are repeated measurements within them. A
density-adjusted measure, such as the observed share divided by a permutation expectation, and an edge correction
belong in the analysis plan before the data are seen.
:::

- **Annotated sources:**
  - @schapiro2017histocat introduced neighbourhood analysis of multiplexed tissue images against a permutation
    reference, the idea behind the observed/expected ratio.
  - @stringer2021cellpose and @greenwald2022mesmer describe pretrained segmentation models, the learning step of the
    chain.
  - @zimmerman2021pseudoreplication shows that cells from one individual are pseudoreplicates and that ignoring this
    inflates type I error.
  - @squair2021pseudobulk demonstrates false discoveries when variation between biological replicates is ignored.
  - @baddeley2005spatstat documents the R tools for spatial point patterns, including edge corrections.
  - @leek2010batch explains how batch effects can masquerade as biology.
  - @eu2017ivdr and @mdcg2019-11 are the binding text and the non-binding guidance for the regulatory paragraph.
